strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple models (GPT-5, Gemini, Claude, Qwen, DeepSeek) and datasets (IMO-GradingBench, Hard2Verify, QiuZhen-Bench) with consistent results
Clear demonstration that pessimistic verification outperforms majority voting for error detection, with better token efficiency than long-CoT scaling
Transparent about trade-offs (TPR decrease) and attempts to explain via dataset annotation analysis
Good presentation with clear figures (Figure 1 and 6) effectively showing efficiency-performance tradeoffs
Contributions of systematic comparison of verification strategies and new high-difficulty dataset (QiuZhen-Bench)
Honest discussion of limitations and case studies showing real instances of disagreement between verifiers and dataset labels
weaknesses: Limited novelty: builds on Liu et al. (2025) with straightforward combinations (simple/vertical/progressive verification); core variants lack fundamental innovation, making this primarily an empirical validation study rather than methodological advance

Insufficient evidence for key claim that 'most false negatives are dataset errors': manual review of only 15-20 cases per model (Table 1) is too small to support extrapolation to widespread mislabeling conclusion
Circular reasoning with QiuZhen-Bench: uses GPT-5 with progressive verification for labeling, then tests the method on the same benchmark, risking that systematic biases get baked into the benchmark
Missing theoretical justification: no formal analysis of why pessimistic verification should outperform majority voting, when it should be preferred, or what conditions enable its effectiveness

Confounded experimental design: different prompts used for different verification types (single-pass vs. chunk verification); ablation studies missing to isolate prompt quality effects from method effects
Manual case review focuses only on false negatives; misses analysis of false positives and true cases, providing incomplete picture of where verifier-annotation disagreements actually occur
Overclaiming in places (e.g., 'state-of-the-art models approach near human experts') without sufficient support
Reproducibility limitations: depends on proprietary models (GPT-5, Gemini) and QiuZhen-Bench construction via GPT-5 labeling creates non-reproducible benchmark without access to GPT-5

strengths: Practical and simple method that can be readily implemented for proof verification tasks
Comprehensive evaluation across three datasets with consistent improvements in TNR and Balanced F1 scores
New high-quality dataset (QiuZhen-Bench) with 1,054 advanced mathematics problems
Demonstrates better token efficiency for test-time scaling compared to long chain-of-thought approaches
Detailed case studies with concrete examples analyzing potential annotation errors
Honest discussion of limitations including acknowledged TPR degradation and potential underestimation effects
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily extends Liu et al. (2025) with straightforward variants; lacks theoretical or methodological innovation suitable for ICML
Unresolved TPR-TNR tradeoff with substantial false positive rates (especially 40-50% TPR loss for weaker models) inadequately justified by manual analysis of only 13-20 cases per model
Circular validation problem: QiuZhen-Bench labeled using the method being evaluated (GPT-5 with progressive@3/6), enabling inflated results and preventing independent validation
Insufficient statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or experiment repetitions reported; some improvements appear modest and potentially non-significant
Incomplete theoretical justification: missing analysis of why pessimistic verification should work, what conditions ensure improvement, and when method should fail
Experimental design gaps: no ablations on hyperparameter choices, limited baseline comparisons (only long-CoT), superficial majority voting analysis without mechanistic explanation
Speculative claims about annotation errors based on limited manual review with subjective categorization (Critical/Minor/Nonsense) lacking independent verification
Scope limitations: evaluated only on mathematical proofs; claims about software engineering applicability unsupported; generalization potential unclear
Reproducibility concerns: many implementation details missing, computational requirements not specified, 'equivalent output tokens' metric non-standard and confusing
Overclaimed conclusions: abstract claims of 'near human expert' performance without systematic measurement; conflation of two distinct claims (method improves detection vs. datasets mislabeled)

strengths: Clear practical contribution showing consistent improvements in error detection (TNR) across multiple models and datasets
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning 9 diverse models and multiple benchmarks with careful efficiency analysis
Honest discussion of dataset annotation issues and limitations, raising important quality concerns
Efficiency gains over long-CoT demonstrated in Figure 1 with significantly fewer equivalent output tokens
Well-structured presentation with effective visualizations and clear methodology
Reproducibility commitment with promised code and dataset release
weaknesses: Limited novelty: explicitly builds on Liu et al. (2025) with only natural extensions of three variants; primarily empirical validation
Insufficient evidence for central claim about annotation errors: only 13-20 manual cases per model reviewed without inter-rater reliability study
Circular validation on QiuZhen-Bench: ground truth labeled by GPT-5 progressive@3/6, the same method being evaluated; not discussed as limitation
No statistical rigor: missing confidence intervals, significance tests, ablation studies, or variance reporting on key results
Inadequate baseline comparisons: only single-pass verification and majority voting; lacks comparison to other ensemble or verification methods
Unexplored TPR-TNR trade-off: significant TPR decreases visible (especially in Figure 6) but no discussion of when this is acceptable for different applications
Missing theoretical justification: unclear why pessimistic outperforms majority voting formally or under what conditions it fails
Dense presentation of results: Figure 6 with 9 models per dataset difficult to parse; critical prompts relegated to appendix

strengths: Clear identification and articulation of error detection as the key verification bottleneck, well-motivated by recent work
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (IMO-GradingBench, Hard2Verify, QiuZhen-Bench) with consistent scaling trends
Significant practical efficiency gains (4× token savings for progressive vs. simple pessimistic verification) validated on state-of-the-art models
Honest and systematic case study analysis revealing annotation errors in established benchmarks (Section 3.4), with detailed examples and discussion
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 1), detailed reproducibility information (prompts, hyperparameters), and promised code release
Validation on real contest problems (IMO 2025, MathArena Apex 2025) demonstrating practical applicability beyond synthetic benchmarks
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core concept (reject if any verifier finds error) is straightforward; variants are largely combinations of existing ideas without theoretical justification

Weak problem-solving validation: small benchmark sizes (6 IMO, 12 MathArena problems), modest absolute improvements (13→22 on 42 points), high variance in results (Figure 7), no statistical significance testing

Dataset annotation error analysis raises more concerns than it resolves: only 20 FN cases per model, subjective classification scheme without inter-rater reliability, circular reasoning risk (using strong model disagreement to 'correct' benchmarks), could bias evaluation in favor of frontier models

QiuZhen-Bench methodology problematic: GPT-5 used for both generation and annotation creating systematic bias, no human verification, only tested on smaller models, introduces new dataset with different distribution complicating interpretation
Missing systematic hyperparameter analysis: prog@3/6 chosen empirically for 'balanced performance' without sensitivity studies; no principled method for selecting n/k for new problems

Incomplete baseline comparisons: long CoT comparison constrained by model capabilities (can't adjust Qwen reasoning_effort), majority voting dismissed quickly, potential unfairness in comparison setup
Limited theoretical grounding: no analysis of why pessimistic verification reduces error rates, no complexity analysis, no formal justification for the approach
High reproducibility barriers: requires expensive access to frontier models and ability to reproduce GPT-5 annotations on custom dataset

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: verification for math reasoning with LLMs
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple datasets and real-world competition problems (IMO 2025, MathArena Apex 2025)
Practical improvements in token efficiency demonstrated alongside accuracy gains (Table 4, Figure 4)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations distinguishing three method variants
Extensive manual case studies providing detailed insight into verification failures
Honest discussion of limitations and annotation quality issues in existing benchmarks
weaknesses: Critical circular logic: Authors claim benchmarks are unreliable for strong models, yet use these benchmarks as primary validation of improvements
Real-world validation severely limited: only 6 IMO problems and 12 Apex problems evaluated without statistical significance testing or confidence intervals

Limited conceptual novelty: 'Pessimistic verification' is a straightforward principle (reject if any verifier finds error); lacks theoretical depth or justification for why it should outperform baselines
No ablation studies on core design choices: binary splitting strategy unexplained; hyperparameter selection (n=3, k=6) appears ad-hoc with no sensitivity analysis
QiuZhen-Bench dataset problematic: uses GPT-5 annotations instead of human experts, then uses this dataset to validate method on weaker models—potential systematic bias
Inconsistent results: Figure 4 shows progressive verification with worse efficiency than simple pessimistic on QiuZhen-Bench initially, suggesting method not robustly superior
Experimental design issues: missing significance tests, no multiple comparison corrections, unfair token accounting, small sample sizes without statistical analysis
Overstated annotation error claims: Table 2 shows 18/20 'nonsense' verdicts for weak models are true negatives, not annotation errors; only 20 cases per model analyzed
Mixed contributions obscure core novelty: paper conflates annotation quality analysis, verification method, and problem-solving workflows into single narrative
Missing key comparisons: no comparison with other hierarchical verification approaches or formal verification methods; no analysis of failure modes

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitations in proof verification for open-ended mathematics
Comprehensive multi-model and multi-dataset experimental validation (11+ models, 3 verification benchmarks, 2 problem-solving benchmarks)
Significant practical efficiency gains: progressive pessimistic verification achieves ~4x token reduction versus simple pessimistic at comparable accuracy
Important meta-contribution: case studies reveal benchmark annotations are unreliable, with stronger models finding legitimate errors missed by annotators
Clear intuitive principle with solid empirical support: error detection is more important than proof acceptance consistency across verifiers
Well-designed progressive decomposition strategy balancing coarse-to-fine verification efficiency and accuracy
Clear presentation with effective figures and comprehensive experimental methodology
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core insight (error detection priority) identified in concurrent work (Pandit et al. 2025), parallel verification used in prior work, progressive subdivision is incremental

Weak theoretical foundation: no formal analysis of why pessimistic combination should outperform alternatives, lack of rigor for claims about rare false negatives in LLMs, no convergence or failure mode analysis

Benchmark annotation reliability undermines validation: discovery that labels are incorrect (Table 2) raises fundamental questions about trustworthiness of reported performance gains; only 20-80 FN cases reviewed per model

Limited problem-solving validation: only 6 problems in IMO 2025 and 12 in MathArena Apex 2025 without error bars or statistical testing; claim of 'remarkable improvements' not strongly supported by sample sizes

Insufficient ablation studies: hyperparameter sensitivity unexplored (choice of n,k appears arbitrary), prompt engineering impact untested despite detailed error-severity policies, no analysis of which error types are better caught
Missing comparative analysis: no comparison with alternative ensemble strategies, confidence-weighted voting, or other decomposition approaches beyond demonstrated baselines
Reproducibility gaps: code URL not provided, chunk selection algorithm for subdivision not fully detailed, token weighting methodology across models unclear
Limited scope of problem-solving experiments restricted to Gemini 3 series while verification experiments tested 11 different models
